_link.title: I can define punishment and distinguish between positive and negative punishment

toLevel2.question: What is the purpose of punishment in operant conditioning?

options.text: To decrease the likelihood of a behaviour recurring
options.explanation: Punishment is defined as any consequence that decreases the likelihood of a behaviour being repeated.

options.text: To increase the likelihood of a behaviour recurring
options.explanation: This describes reinforcement, not punishment. Reinforcement increases behaviour; punishment decreases it.

options.text: To maintain the current rate of a behaviour
options.explanation: Punishment does not maintain behaviour; it aims to decrease the likelihood of the behaviour recurring.

options.text: To replace one behaviour with a different behaviour
options.explanation: Punishment decreases a behaviour but does not specifically replace it with another behaviour.

options.text: Adding an undesirable stimulus to decrease behaviour
options.explanation: Positive punishment involves the addition of an aversive or undesirable stimulus, which decreases the likelihood of the behaviour recurring.

options.text: Removing a desirable stimulus to decrease behaviour
options.explanation: This describes negative punishment, which involves the removal of something pleasant to decrease behaviour.

options.text: Adding a desirable stimulus to increase behaviour
options.explanation: This describes positive reinforcement, which increases behaviour by adding something pleasant.

options.text: Removing an undesirable stimulus to increase behaviour
options.explanation: This describes negative reinforcement, which increases behaviour by removing something aversive.

toLevel2.question: Which term is another name for negative punishment?

options.explanation: Negative punishment is also referred to as response cost because something desirable is taken away as a cost of the behaviour.
Positive reinforcement involves adding a desirable stimulus to increase behaviour, which is different from negative punishment.
Aversive conditioning is a broader term and does not specifically refer to negative punishment.
Escape learning is related to negative reinforcement, where behaviour increases to remove an aversive stimulus.

options.text: Removing a desirable stimulus to decrease behaviour
options.explanation: Negative punishment involves the removal of something pleasant or desirable, which decreases the likelihood of the behaviour recurring.

options.text: Adding an undesirable stimulus to decrease behaviour
options.explanation: This describes positive punishment, which adds something aversive to decrease behaviour.

options.text: Removing an undesirable stimulus to increase behaviour
options.explanation: This describes negative reinforcement, not negative punishment.

options.text: Adding a desirable stimulus to increase behaviour
options.explanation: This describes positive reinforcement, not negative punishment.

toLevel2.question: In operant conditioning, what effect does punishment have on a behaviour?

options.text: It decreases the likelihood of the behaviour
options.explanation: Punishment is any consequence that decreases the likelihood of a behaviour recurring.

options.text: It increases the likelihood of the behaviour
options.explanation: Increasing behaviour is the function of reinforcement, not punishment.

options.text: It has no effect on the likelihood of behaviour
options.explanation: By definition, punishment does have an effect — it decreases the likelihood of a behaviour recurring.

options.text: It eliminates the behaviour permanently from now
options.explanation: Punishment decreases the likelihood of a behaviour recurring, but does not necessarily eliminate it permanently.

toLevel2.question: Positive punishment involves adding an undesirable stimulus to decrease the likelihood of a behaviour recurring.

options.explanation: Positive punishment is defined as adding (positive) an aversive or undesirable stimulus, which decreases the likelihood of the behaviour recurring.
This statement is correct. Positive punishment involves adding an undesirable stimulus to decrease behaviour.

toLevel2.question: Negative punishment involves adding an undesirable stimulus to decrease the likelihood of a behaviour recurring.

options.explanation: Negative punishment involves removing a desirable stimulus, not adding an undesirable one. Adding an undesirable stimulus describes positive punishment.
Negative punishment involves removing a desirable stimulus, not adding an undesirable one. Adding an undesirable stimulus describes positive punishment.

toLevel2.question: Punishment is any consequence that {{blank:1}} the likelihood of a behaviour recurring.

options.explanation: Punishment is defined as any consequence that decreases the likelihood of a behaviour recurring.
Increasing the likelihood of a behaviour describes reinforcement, not punishment.
Punishment does not maintain behaviour; it decreases the likelihood of the behaviour recurring.

toLevel2.question: Positive punishment involves {{blank:1}} an undesirable stimulus to decrease behaviour.

options.explanation: In positive punishment, an aversive or undesirable stimulus is added to decrease the likelihood of the behaviour recurring.
Removing a stimulus describes negative punishment or negative reinforcement, not positive punishment.
Ignoring a stimulus does not describe positive punishment. Positive punishment requires adding an undesirable stimulus.

toLevel2.question: Negative punishment involves {{blank:1}} a desirable stimulus to decrease behaviour.

options.explanation: Negative punishment involves removing something pleasant or desirable, which decreases the likelihood of the behaviour recurring.
Adding a stimulus describes positive punishment or positive reinforcement, not negative punishment.
Pairing stimuli is associated with classical conditioning, not negative punishment in operant conditioning.

toLevel3.question: Why is the word 'positive' used in positive punishment?

options.text: Because a stimulus is added to the situation
options.explanation: In operant conditioning, 'positive' refers to the addition of a stimulus. Positive punishment adds an undesirable stimulus to decrease behaviour.

options.text: Because the outcome is good for the learner
options.explanation: 'Positive' does not mean pleasant. It refers to the addition of a stimulus, regardless of whether the experience is pleasant.

options.text: Because it involves a reward for good conduct
options.explanation: Positive punishment does not involve a reward. It involves adding something aversive to decrease behaviour.

options.text: Because the behaviour becomes more frequent
options.explanation: Punishment decreases behaviour. The word 'positive' refers to the addition of a stimulus, not an increase in behaviour.

toLevel3.question: How does negative punishment differ from positive punishment?

options.text: Negative punishment removes a desirable stimulus rather than adding an undesirable one
options.explanation: Positive punishment adds something aversive; negative punishment removes something pleasant. Both aim to decrease the likelihood of a behaviour recurring.

options.text: Negative punishment increases behaviour while positive punishment decreases it
options.explanation: Both types of punishment decrease behaviour. They differ in whether a stimulus is added or removed.

options.text: Negative punishment uses verbal feedback while positive punishment uses physical action
options.explanation: The distinction is not about the form of the stimulus. It is about whether a stimulus is added or removed.

options.text: Negative punishment is less effective at changing behaviour than positive punishment
options.explanation: The distinction between positive and negative punishment is about whether a stimulus is added or removed, not about effectiveness.

toLevel3.question: What do positive punishment and negative punishment have in common?

options.text: Both decrease the likelihood of a behaviour recurring
options.explanation: All forms of punishment share the goal of decreasing the likelihood of a behaviour being repeated, whether by adding or removing a stimulus.

options.text: Both involve removing something from the environment
options.explanation: Only negative punishment involves removal. Positive punishment involves adding a stimulus.

options.text: Both involve adding something to the environment
options.explanation: Only positive punishment involves adding a stimulus. Negative punishment involves removing a stimulus.

options.text: Both increase the likelihood of a behaviour recurring
options.explanation: Increasing behaviour is the function of reinforcement, not punishment. Both types of punishment decrease behaviour.

toLevel3.question: Which statement best explains why negative punishment is also called response cost?

options.text: Because performing the behaviour costs the learner something desirable
options.explanation: The term 'response cost' indicates that the learner pays a cost — losing something they value — as a consequence of their behaviour.

options.text: Because the punishment involves a financial penalty every time
options.explanation: 'Cost' does not necessarily mean money. It refers broadly to the loss of any desirable stimulus as a consequence of behaviour.

options.text: Because it costs the teacher effort to implement the punishment
options.explanation: Response cost refers to the cost borne by the learner, not the effort required by the person delivering the punishment.

options.text: Because the behaviour is too costly to the learner to continue
options.explanation: While the outcome may be that the behaviour decreases, the term 'response cost' specifically refers to the removal of a desirable stimulus.

toLevel3.question: How does punishment differ from reinforcement in operant conditioning?

options.text: Punishment decreases behaviour while reinforcement increases behaviour
options.explanation: The key distinction is the effect on behaviour: punishment decreases the likelihood of a behaviour recurring, while reinforcement increases it.

options.text: Punishment always involves pain while reinforcement always involves pleasure
options.explanation: Punishment and reinforcement are defined by their effect on behaviour, not by whether they cause pain or pleasure.

options.text: Punishment is used with animals while reinforcement is used with humans
options.explanation: Both punishment and reinforcement apply to both human and animal learning in operant conditioning.

options.text: Punishment involves voluntary behaviour while reinforcement involves involuntary behaviour
options.explanation: Both punishment and reinforcement operate on voluntary behaviour in operant conditioning.

toLevel3.question: Why is it important to understand that 'negative' in negative punishment refers to removal?

options.text: Because students often confuse 'negative' with 'bad' rather than 'taking away'
options.explanation: A common misconception is that 'negative' means harmful or bad. In operant conditioning, 'negative' specifically means the removal of a stimulus.

options.text: Because 'negative' indicates the punishment does not work effectively
options.explanation: 'Negative' does not refer to effectiveness. It refers to the removal of a stimulus from the environment.

options.text: Because 'negative' means the learner feels bad about the consequence
options.explanation: 'Negative' refers to the removal of a stimulus, not the learner's emotional response to the punishment.

options.text: Because 'negative' refers to the learner's attitude toward school
options.explanation: 'Negative' in this context has a specific technical meaning — the removal of a stimulus — and does not relate to attitudes.

toLevel3.question: In operant conditioning, the word 'positive' in positive punishment means that something is added to the situation, not that the experience is pleasant.

options.explanation: 'Positive' in operant conditioning refers to the addition of a stimulus. In positive punishment, an undesirable stimulus is added, so the experience is not pleasant.
The statement is correct. 'Positive' refers to adding a stimulus, not to the pleasantness of the experience.

toLevel3.question: In operant conditioning, 'positive' means a stimulus is {{blank:1}}, while 'negative' means a stimulus is {{blank:2}}.

options.explanation: 'Positive' in operant conditioning refers to the addition of a stimulus to the environment.
Removal of a stimulus is described by the term 'negative', not 'positive'.
'Positive' does not mean ignored. It specifically means a stimulus is added to the environment.
'Negative' in operant conditioning refers to the removal of a stimulus from the environment.
Addition of a stimulus is described by the term 'positive', not 'negative'.
'Negative' does not mean repeated. It specifically means a stimulus is removed from the environment.

toLevel3.question: Both positive and negative punishment share the same effect on behaviour: they both {{blank:1}} the likelihood of the behaviour recurring.

options.explanation: All forms of punishment decrease the likelihood of a behaviour recurring, whether through adding or removing a stimulus.
Increasing behaviour is the function of reinforcement, not punishment.
Punishment does not maintain behaviour. Its defining characteristic is that it decreases behaviour.

toLevel3.question: Negative punishment is also known as {{blank:1}} because performing the behaviour costs the learner something desirable.

options.explanation: Negative punishment is also called response cost because the learner loses something valued as a consequence of their behaviour.
Escape learning is associated with negative reinforcement, not negative punishment.
Stimulus control refers to a behaviour being influenced by the presence of a particular stimulus, not to negative punishment.

toLevel4.question: Priya's teacher gives her extra homework after she talks during class, and Priya stops talking in class. Which type of consequence has occurred?

options.explanation: An undesirable stimulus (extra homework) was added following Priya's behaviour, and the behaviour decreased. This is positive punishment.
Negative punishment involves removing a desirable stimulus. Here, extra homework was added, not removed.
Positive reinforcement adds a desirable stimulus to increase behaviour. Priya's talking decreased, not increased.
Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus to increase behaviour. Here, a stimulus was added and behaviour decreased.

toLevel4.question: After Kofi repeatedly breaks curfew, his parents take away his gaming console for a week. Kofi stops breaking curfew. Which consequence type does this illustrate?

options.explanation: A desirable stimulus (gaming console) was removed following Kofi's behaviour, and the behaviour decreased. This is negative punishment.
Positive punishment involves adding an undesirable stimulus. Here, a desirable stimulus was removed.
Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus to increase behaviour. Here, a desirable stimulus was removed and behaviour decreased.
Positive reinforcement adds a desirable stimulus to increase behaviour. Here, a stimulus was removed and behaviour decreased.

toLevel4.question: Mei receives a verbal reprimand from her coach every time she arrives late to training. She begins arriving on time. Which type of punishment is the coach using?

options.explanation: A verbal reprimand is an undesirable stimulus that was added after Mei's late arrival, and her lateness decreased. This is positive punishment.
Negative punishment involves removing a desirable stimulus, not adding a verbal reprimand.
Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus to increase behaviour, which does not match this scenario.
Positive reinforcement adds a desirable stimulus to increase behaviour. A reprimand is not desirable and the target behaviour decreased.

toLevel4.question: After Anika uses her phone during class, the teacher removes her free-time privileges for the rest of the day. Anika stops using her phone in class. What type of consequence is this?

options.explanation: Free-time privileges (a desirable stimulus) were removed following the behaviour, and the behaviour decreased. This is negative punishment (response cost).
Positive punishment involves adding an undesirable stimulus. Here, a desirable stimulus was removed.
Positive reinforcement adds a desirable stimulus to increase behaviour. Anika's phone use decreased, not increased.
Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus to increase behaviour. Here, a desirable stimulus was removed and behaviour decreased.

toLevel4.question: Tariq's dog jumps on visitors. Tariq sprays the dog with water each time it jumps, and the dog stops jumping on visitors. Which consequence type is Tariq using?

options.explanation: An undesirable stimulus (water spray) was added after the jumping behaviour, and the behaviour decreased. This is positive punishment.
Negative punishment involves removing a desirable stimulus. Here, an aversive stimulus was added.
Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus to increase behaviour. Here, an aversive stimulus was added and behaviour decreased.
Positive reinforcement adds a desirable stimulus to increase behaviour. Water spray is not desirable and the behaviour decreased.

toLevel4.question: Lena's parents reduce her weekly allowance each time she leaves her room messy. Lena begins keeping her room tidy. What consequence type does this scenario demonstrate?

options.explanation: A desirable stimulus (allowance money) was removed following the messy behaviour, and the behaviour decreased. This is negative punishment (response cost).
Positive punishment involves adding an undesirable stimulus. Here, money was removed rather than something being added.
Positive reinforcement adds a desirable stimulus to increase behaviour. Here, something desirable was removed.
Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus to increase behaviour. Here, a desirable stimulus was removed and the messy behaviour decreased.

toLevel4.question: Jamal talks back to his teacher and is given a detention. He stops talking back in class. This is an example of which type of consequence?

options.explanation: An undesirable stimulus (detention) was added after the talking-back behaviour, and the behaviour decreased. This is positive punishment.
Negative punishment involves removing a desirable stimulus. Here, detention was added.
Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus to increase behaviour, which does not match this scenario.
Positive reinforcement adds a desirable stimulus to increase behaviour. Detention is not desirable and the behaviour decreased.

toLevel4.question: When Yuki's parents take away her tablet after she refuses to do homework, they are using {{blank:1}} because a desirable stimulus has been {{blank:2}}.

options.explanation: Removing a desirable stimulus (the tablet) to decrease behaviour (refusing homework) is negative punishment.
Positive punishment involves adding an undesirable stimulus, not removing a desirable one.
Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus to increase behaviour, which is not what is happening here.
In negative punishment, a desirable stimulus is removed to decrease the likelihood of the behaviour recurring.
Adding a stimulus describes positive punishment or positive reinforcement, not negative punishment.
Pairing stimuli is associated with classical conditioning, not negative punishment in operant conditioning.

toLevel4.question: When a coach makes an athlete run extra laps for breaking a rule, and the athlete stops breaking the rule, the coach has used {{blank:1}} because an undesirable stimulus was {{blank:2}}.

options.explanation: An undesirable stimulus (extra laps) was added and the behaviour decreased, which defines positive punishment.
Negative punishment involves removing a desirable stimulus, not adding extra laps.
Positive reinforcement adds a desirable stimulus to increase behaviour, not an undesirable stimulus to decrease it.
In positive punishment, an undesirable stimulus is added to the situation to decrease the behaviour.
Removing a stimulus describes negative punishment or negative reinforcement, not positive punishment.
Positive punishment requires the addition of a stimulus, not ignoring the behaviour.

toLevel4.question: Omar's friends criticise him every time he interrupts during conversation, and he stops interrupting. The criticism serves as {{blank:1}} because it is an undesirable stimulus that has been {{blank:2}} to decrease behaviour.

options.explanation: Criticism is an undesirable stimulus that was added, and the interrupting behaviour decreased. This is positive punishment.
Negative punishment involves removing a desirable stimulus, not adding criticism.
Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus to increase behaviour, not what is occurring here.
In positive punishment, an undesirable stimulus is added to decrease the likelihood of the behaviour recurring.
Removing a stimulus describes negative processes in operant conditioning, not positive punishment.
Positive punishment involves the addition of a stimulus, not maintaining a constant environment.

toLevel5.question: A student argues that grounding a teenager is positive punishment because it is a harsh consequence. What is the flaw in this reasoning?

options.text: Grounding removes freedoms rather than adding a stimulus, making it negative punishment
options.explanation: Grounding removes the teenager's freedom or privileges (a desirable stimulus), which is negative punishment. 'Positive' refers to addition, not severity.

options.text: Grounding is not a form of punishment because it does not cause physical harm
options.explanation: Punishment does not require physical harm. Grounding is punishment because it decreases behaviour, specifically negative punishment.

options.text: Grounding is actually reinforcement because the teenager learns from the experience
options.explanation: Grounding decreases behaviour, making it punishment. Learning occurs through both reinforcement and punishment.

options.text: The student is correct because grounding is a severe and unpleasant consequence
options.explanation: 'Positive' in operant conditioning refers to adding a stimulus, not to severity. Grounding removes freedoms, so it is negative punishment.

toLevel5.question: A researcher observes that a child's aggressive behaviour decreases after the child loses access to a favourite toy each time aggression occurs. Which analysis correctly identifies the consequence type and mechanism?

options.text: This is negative punishment because a desirable stimulus is removed and behaviour decreases
options.explanation: The favourite toy (desirable stimulus) is removed following aggression, and the aggression decreases. This matches the definition of negative punishment.

options.text: This is positive punishment because losing a toy is an unpleasant experience for the child
options.explanation: The unpleasantness of the experience does not determine the type. The mechanism is removal of a desirable stimulus, which is negative punishment.

options.text: This is negative reinforcement because the child learns to avoid negative outcomes
options.explanation: Negative reinforcement increases behaviour by removing an aversive stimulus. Here, behaviour decreased and a desirable stimulus was removed.

options.text: This is positive reinforcement because the child learns a valuable lesson from it
options.explanation: Positive reinforcement adds a desirable stimulus to increase behaviour. The child's aggressive behaviour decreased following loss of a toy.

toLevel5.question: A teacher gives students extra cleaning duties when they misbehave, but some students continue to misbehave at the same rate. Can the extra cleaning duties still be classified as positive punishment?

options.text: No, because punishment is defined by a decrease in behaviour, which has not occurred
options.explanation: Punishment must decrease behaviour to be classified as punishment. If the behaviour continues at the same rate, the consequence is not functioning as punishment.

options.text: Yes, because an undesirable stimulus has been added to the situation regardless
options.explanation: Simply adding an undesirable stimulus is not sufficient. The consequence must also decrease behaviour to qualify as punishment.

options.text: Yes, because the teacher intends it to be a punishment for those students
options.explanation: Punishment is defined by its effect on behaviour, not by the intention of the person delivering it.

options.text: No, because cleaning duties are a form of negative reinforcement for the students
options.explanation: The reason it is not punishment is that behaviour has not decreased. Cleaning duties are not negative reinforcement in this scenario.

toLevel5.question: Amara receives a fine for speeding and stops speeding. Her friend Dele also receives a fine but continues to speed. What does this comparison reveal about punishment?

options.text: Whether a consequence functions as punishment depends on its effect on the individual's behaviour
options.explanation: Punishment is defined by a decrease in behaviour. The same consequence may function as punishment for one person but not another, depending on whether behaviour decreases.

options.text: Fines are an unreliable form of punishment and should not be used as consequences
options.explanation: The comparison shows that punishment effectiveness varies between individuals, not that fines are inherently unreliable.

options.text: Amara experienced negative punishment while Dele experienced positive punishment
options.explanation: Both received the same consequence (a fine, which removes money — negative punishment). The difference is in whether the behaviour decreased.

options.text: Dele must not have understood that the fine was meant as a punishment for him
options.explanation: Punishment is defined by its effect on behaviour, not by whether the individual understands its purpose.

toLevel5.question: A psychology student claims that taking away a child's dessert to stop tantrums is positive punishment because the child is upset. What error has the student made?

options.text: The student confused emotional response with the mechanism; removing dessert is negative punishment
options.explanation: The child's emotional response does not determine the type. Removing dessert (a desirable stimulus) to decrease tantrums is negative punishment, regardless of how upset the child becomes.

options.text: The student is correct because the child's distress confirms it is positive punishment
options.explanation: 'Positive' refers to adding a stimulus, not to the child's distress. Removing dessert is negative punishment.

options.text: The student confused punishment with reinforcement since the child may tantrum more
options.explanation: If the tantrums decrease, it is punishment. The error is in confusing positive and negative, not punishment and reinforcement.

options.text: The student is correct because any consequence that causes distress is positive punishment
options.explanation: 'Positive' refers to addition of a stimulus, not to causing distress. Removing dessert is removal, making it negative punishment.

toLevel5.question: In a workplace, an employee who arrives late is publicly reprimanded and also loses their flexible work arrangement. Which types of punishment are being applied?

options.text: Both positive punishment and negative punishment are applied together
options.explanation: The public reprimand adds an undesirable stimulus (positive punishment), while losing the flexible arrangement removes a desirable stimulus (negative punishment).

options.text: Only positive punishment is applied because both consequences are unpleasant
options.explanation: The type of punishment is determined by whether a stimulus is added or removed, not by how unpleasant the experience is.

options.text: Only negative punishment is applied because the employee loses something valued
options.explanation: The reprimand is an added stimulus (positive punishment), while the loss of flexibility is removal of a desirable stimulus (negative punishment). Both types are present.

options.text: Neither type of punishment applies because workplace consequences are not operant conditioning
options.explanation: Operant conditioning principles apply to workplace settings. Both positive and negative punishment are being used here.

toLevel5.question: A parent argues that smacking a child is the most effective form of positive punishment. Which evaluation of this claim is most psychologically accurate?

options.text: While smacking is positive punishment, research shows physical punishment can have harmful side effects beyond the intended behaviour change
options.explanation: Smacking adds an aversive stimulus (positive punishment), but research indicates it can produce aggression, anxiety, and damaged relationships beyond simply decreasing the targeted behaviour.

options.text: Smacking is not positive punishment because it does not involve adding a pleasant stimulus to the situation
options.explanation: 'Positive' in positive punishment means adding a stimulus, not adding something pleasant. Smacking does add an aversive stimulus.

options.text: Smacking is negative punishment because it removes the child's sense of safety and wellbeing
options.explanation: Smacking adds a physical stimulus; it is classified based on the addition of the stimulus, making it positive punishment.

options.text: The parent is entirely correct because physical punishment always produces the fastest behaviour change
options.explanation: Research does not support the claim that physical punishment is always the most effective. It can also produce harmful side effects.

toLevel5.question: Two teachers debate whether removing recess is positive or negative punishment. Teacher A says it is negative punishment; Teacher B says it is positive because children dislike missing recess. Who is correct?

options.text: Teacher A, because recess is a desirable stimulus being removed
options.explanation: Removing recess takes away a desirable stimulus to decrease behaviour, which is negative punishment. 'Positive' and 'negative' refer to addition and removal, not to how the child feels.

options.text: Teacher B, because the children experience distress when recess is removed
options.explanation: The children's distress does not determine the type. The classification depends on whether a stimulus is added or removed.

options.text: Both are correct because it depends on the individual child's perception
options.explanation: The classification is based on the mechanism (adding vs removing), not the child's perception. Removing recess is negative punishment.

options.text: Neither is correct because removing recess is a form of negative reinforcement
options.explanation: Negative reinforcement increases behaviour. Removing recess decreases behaviour, making it negative punishment. Teacher A is correct.

toLevel5.question: When a consequence is intended to decrease behaviour but the behaviour does not change, the consequence cannot be classified as {{blank:1}} because punishment is defined by its {{blank:2}} on behaviour.

options.explanation: Punishment is defined by its effect — a decrease in behaviour. If behaviour does not decrease, the consequence is not functioning as punishment.
Reinforcement increases behaviour. The scenario describes an intended decrease, so the relevant term is punishment.
Conditioning is a broader term. The specific concept being tested is whether a consequence qualifies as punishment based on its effect.
Punishment is defined by its effect on behaviour — specifically, a decrease in the likelihood of the behaviour recurring.
Punishment is not defined by the intention behind it, but by whether the behaviour actually decreases.
The severity of a consequence does not determine whether it is punishment. The defining criterion is its effect on behaviour.

toLevel5.question: A common error when classifying punishment is confusing the {{blank:1}} of the experience with the {{blank:2}} of the consequence, which is whether a stimulus is added or removed.

options.explanation: Students often confuse how pleasant or unpleasant an experience feels with the mechanism of the consequence (addition or removal of a stimulus).
The mechanism (adding or removing) is what should be used to classify. The error involves confusing emotional quality with mechanism.
The common classification error involves emotional quality, not the frequency of the consequence.
The mechanism — whether a stimulus is added (positive) or removed (negative) — is the correct basis for classifying the type of punishment.
Intensity is not the defining feature. The mechanism (adding or removing a stimulus) determines whether punishment is positive or negative.
Duration is not the defining feature for classification. The mechanism (adding or removing) determines positive or negative punishment.
